input: Research accessible bathroom modifications for aging parents

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Knowing which specific mobility or safety challenges the parents face (e.g., balance issues, wheelchair use, limited grip strength) determines which modifications are actually relevant — grab bars vs. roll-in showers vs. raised toilets are very different projects.
Whether the user is researching to advise parents from a distance, coordinate with a contractor, or present options to a family decision-maker changes the depth and format of research needed.
Whether the parents own or rent their home, and the bathroom's current layout (e.g., tub-only, small footprint), directly limits which modifications are feasible at all.
The budget range radically changes the solution set — a $500 project (grab bars, non-slip mats) vs. a $10,000+ remodel (walk-in shower, widened doorways) are entirely different research paths.
Whether the user wants a simple summary list, a comparison of products/contractors, or a step-by-step action plan determines how the research output should be structured.
Understanding the end goal — e.g., preventing falls, enabling independent living, preparing for a specific diagnosis — clarifies what 'good enough' looks like and when the research is done.
Whether the parents prioritize aesthetics and minimal visible change vs. maximum safety functionality affects which product styles and modification approaches to highlight.

gold.taskTitle: Research accessible bathroom mods for aging parents
gold.taskDescription: Find and evaluate bathroom modification options that improve safety and accessibility for the user's aging parents.

questions.title: What mobility or health challenges do your parents currently have?
questions.description: Identify the specific physical limitations (e.g., balance issues, walker/wheelchair use, arthritis, post-surgery recovery) driving the need for modifications.

questions.title: Who will act on this research once it is done?
questions.description: Clarify whether the user will present options to parents, hire a contractor directly, or coordinate with other family members — this shapes the required depth and format.

questions.title: Do your parents own their home, and what is the bathroom layout?
questions.description: Determine ownership status and basic layout (tub vs. shower, doorway width, square footage) to filter out modifications that are not structurally or legally feasible.

questions.title: What is the approximate budget available for modifications?
questions.description: Establish a rough spending range to scope research between low-cost add-ons (grab bars, mats) and larger renovations (walk-in shower, widened doorways).

questions.title: What should the final research output look like?
questions.description: Determine the desired deliverable — a ranked product list, a contractor checklist, a cost comparison table, or a simple summary of options.

questions.title: What does a successful outcome look like for your parents?
questions.description: Pin down the primary goal — fall prevention, maintaining full independence, preparing for a progressive condition, or satisfying a doctor's recommendation.

questions.title: How important is appearance versus maximum safety functionality?
questions.description: Understand whether parents want modifications that blend in aesthetically or are willing to prioritize clinical-grade safety features over looks.
